identity.title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.

content.abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.
